<div class="container">
    <div class="page-header">
        <div class="breadcrumb">
            <a href="/">Home</a> / <a href="/guides/">Guides</a> / EDR vs XDR
        </div>
        <h1><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> EDR vs XDR: The Complete Security Guide</h1>
        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem;">Understanding the Evolution from Endpoint Security
            to Extended Detection</p>
        <div class="page-meta">
            <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 22 min read</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Beginner to Intermediate</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> December 2025</span>
        </div>
    </div>

    <!-- Featured Image -->
    <div class="featured-image">
        <img src="/images/guides/edr-vs-xdr.png"
            alt="EDR vs XDR comparison showing endpoint detection versus extended detection across multiple security layers"
            width="800" height="450" loading="lazy">
    </div>

    <div class="content">
        <!-- Table of Contents -->
        <div class="toc">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-list-ul"></i> Table of Contents</h3>
            <ul>
                <li><a href="#introduction">1. Introduction: Beyond the Acronyms</a></li>
                <li><a href="#what-is-edr">2. What is EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)?</a></li>
                <li><a href="#what-is-xdr">3. What is XDR (Extended Detection and Response)?</a></li>
                <li><a href="#key-differences">4. EDR vs XDR: The Core Differences</a></li>
                <li><a href="#evolution">5. The Security Evolution: From AV to EDR to XDR</a></li>
                <li><a href="#real-attacks">6. How Each Handles Real Attacks</a></li>
                <li><a href="#hidden-costs">7. The Hidden Costs Nobody Talks About</a></li>
                <li><a href="#decision-framework">8. Decision Framework: Which One Do You Actually Need?</a></li>
                <li><a href="#vendor-landscape">9. The Vendor Landscape in 2025</a></li>
                <li><a href="#migration-path">10. The Migration Path: EDR to XDR</a></li>
                <li><a href="#key-takeaways">11. Key Takeaways</a></li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <h2 id="introduction">1. Introduction: Beyond the Acronyms</h2>
        <p>
            Every security vendor claims their product is "next-gen." The alphabet soup of EDR, XDR, MDR, and NDR
            has
            made it nearly impossible for security professionals to cut through the marketing noise and understand
            what they actually need.
        </p>
        <p>
            Here's the truth most vendors won't tell you: <strong>XDR isn't always better than EDR</strong>. And EDR
            isn't "legacy" technology that needs replacing. The right choice depends entirely on your organization's
            maturity, infrastructure, and operational reality.
        </p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> The Real Question</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                Stop asking "EDR or XDR?" and start asking: "What's my detection coverage gap, and what's the most
                operationally sustainable way to close it?"
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="what-is-edr">2. What is EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response)?</h2>
        <p>
            <strong>Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)</strong> solutions focus on monitoring, detecting, and
            responding to threats on endpoints—laptops, desktops, servers, and mobile devices. Think of EDR as
            having a security camera on every computer in your organization.
        </p>

        <h3>Core EDR Capabilities</h3>
        <div class="feature-grid">
            <div class="feature-card">
                <div class="feature-icon"><i class="fas fa-eye"></i></div>
                <div class="feature-title">Continuous Monitoring</div>
                <p>Records process executions, file changes, network connections, and registry modifications 24/7
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="feature-card">
                <div class="feature-icon"><i class="fas fa-search"></i></div>
                <div class="feature-title">Threat Detection</div>
                <p>Uses behavioral analysis and IOC matching to identify suspicious activity in real-time</p>
            </div>
            <div class="feature-card">
                <div class="feature-icon"><i class="fas fa-tasks"></i></div>
                <div class="feature-title">Investigation Tools</div>
                <p>Process trees, timeline analysis, and forensic data for deep-dive investigations</p>
            </div>
            <div class="feature-card">
                <div class="feature-icon"><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i></div>
                <div class="feature-title">Response Actions</div>
                <p>Isolate hosts, kill processes, quarantine files, and run remediation scripts remotely</p>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>What EDR Actually Records</h3>
        <p>
            Modern EDR solutions capture an enormous amount of telemetry from each endpoint:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Process telemetry:</strong> Parent-child relationships, command-line arguments, file hashes
            </li>
            <li><strong>File system activity:</strong> Create, modify, delete, and rename operations</li>
            <li><strong>Network connections:</strong> Inbound/outbound connections with destination IPs and ports
            </li>
            <li><strong>Registry changes:</strong> Key modifications, especially in persistence locations</li>
            <li><strong>Authentication events:</strong> Logon attempts, credential usage, privilege escalation</li>
            <li><strong>Loaded modules:</strong> DLLs, drivers, and injected code</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> EDR Strength</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                EDR excels at answering "What happened on this specific machine?" with surgical precision.
                For endpoint-focused threats like ransomware, commodity malware, and insider threats, EDR
                provides unmatched visibility.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="what-is-xdr">3. What is XDR (Extended Detection and Response)?</h2>
        <p>
            <strong>Extended Detection and Response (XDR)</strong> expands detection and response beyond endpoints
            to include network traffic, cloud workloads, email, identity systems, and more. XDR correlates data
            across multiple security layers to detect sophisticated attacks that span the entire kill chain.
        </p>
        <p>
            Think of EDR as a security camera on each computer, while XDR is an integrated security command center
            with cameras everywhere—inside computers, on the network, in the cloud, at the email gateway, and
            watching user identities.
        </p>

        <h3>XDR Data Sources</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Layer</th>
                    <th>Data Sources</th>
                    <th>Detection Examples</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Endpoint</strong></td>
                    <td>EDR telemetry, AV logs, OS events</td>
                    <td>Malware execution, lateral movement</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Network</strong></td>
                    <td>NDR, firewall, DNS, proxy logs</td>
                    <td>C2 communication, data exfiltration</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Cloud</strong></td>
                    <td>AWS CloudTrail, Azure AD, M365</td>
                    <td>Impossible travel, suspicious API calls</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Email</strong></td>
                    <td>Email gateway, O365 protection</td>
                    <td>Phishing, BEC, credential harvesting</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Identity</strong></td>
                    <td>AD, Okta, Azure AD, privileged access</td>
                    <td>Credential abuse, privilege escalation</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>How XDR Correlates Attacks</h3>
        <p>
            The power of XDR is correlation. Instead of seeing isolated alerts, XDR connects the dots across
            multiple data sources to tell a complete attack story:
        </p>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Email layer:</strong> Phishing email delivered to user@company.com</li>
            <li><strong>Endpoint layer:</strong> User opens attachment, PowerShell downloads payload</li>
            <li><strong>Network layer:</strong> Outbound connection to known C2 infrastructure</li>
            <li><strong>Identity layer:</strong> Credential theft detected, lateral movement to server</li>
            <li><strong>Cloud layer:</strong> Unusual data download from SharePoint</li>
        </ol>
        <p>
            With EDR alone, you might see step 2. With XDR, you see the entire attack and can respond
            comprehensively.
        </p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Native vs. Open XDR</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                <strong>Native XDR</strong> (single-vendor) integrates tightly with one vendor's product suite.
                <strong>Open XDR</strong> (hybrid) integrates with multi-vendor environments through APIs and data
                connectors.
                Choose based on your existing security stack.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="key-differences">4. EDR vs XDR: The Core Differences</h2>

        <div class="comparison-grid">
            <div class="comparison-card edr">
                <h4><i class="fas fa-laptop"></i> EDR</h4>
                <ul>
                    <li>Endpoint-focused visibility</li>
                    <li>Deep telemetry on each device</li>
                    <li>Fast deployment (agents only)</li>
                    <li>Lower total cost of ownership</li>
                    <li>Simpler to operationalize</li>
                    <li>Best for endpoint-centric threats</li>
                </ul>
            </div>
            <div class="comparison-card xdr">
                <h4><i class="fas fa-project-diagram"></i> XDR</h4>
                <ul>
                    <li>Cross-layer visibility</li>
                    <li>Attack correlation across sources</li>
                    <li>Complex deployment (integrations)</li>
                    <li>Higher TCO but broader coverage</li>
                    <li>Requires mature security ops</li>
                    <li>Best for sophisticated attacks</li>
                </ul>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>Detailed Comparison</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Aspect</th>
                    <th>EDR</th>
                    <th>XDR</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Data Sources</strong></td>
                    <td>Endpoints only</td>
                    <td>Endpoints + Network + Cloud + Email + Identity</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Detection Scope</strong></td>
                    <td>Single device analysis</td>
                    <td>Cross-domain correlation</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Alert Volume</strong></td>
                    <td>High (siloed alerts)</td>
                    <td>Lower (correlated incidents)</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Investigation</strong></td>
                    <td>"What happened on this host?"</td>
                    <td>"What's the full attack story?"</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Response</strong></td>
                    <td>Endpoint actions only</td>
                    <td>Cross-platform orchestration</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Deployment Time</strong></td>
                    <td>Days to weeks</td>
                    <td>Weeks to months</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Staff Required</strong></td>
                    <td>1-2 security analysts</td>
                    <td>Full SOC team recommended</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Price Range</strong></td>
                    <td>$5-15/endpoint/month</td>
                    <td>$15-50/user/month (varies widely)</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="evolution">5. The Security Evolution: From AV to EDR to XDR</h2>
        <p>
            Understanding how we got here helps clarify where each technology fits:
        </p>

        <div class="evolution-timeline">
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <div class="timeline-year">1990s-2000s: Antivirus Era</div>
                <p>
                    Signature-based detection. Scan files, match known malware hashes, quarantine threats.
                    Worked well when threats were relatively simple and spread slowly via floppy disks and email
                    attachments.
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <div class="timeline-year">2013-2015: EDR Emerges</div>
                <p>
                    Carbon Black, CrowdStrike, and Cylance pioneered endpoint detection. Behavioral analysis
                    replaced
                    signature-only approaches. Security teams gained visibility into <em>how</em> attacks happen,
                    not just <em>what</em> files were malicious.
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <div class="timeline-year">2018-2020: XDR Concept Introduced</div>
                <p>
                    Palo Alto Networks coined "XDR" in 2018. The idea: correlate telemetry across multiple security
                    layers to detect sophisticated attacks. Initially more marketing than reality.
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="timeline-item">
                <div class="timeline-year">2021-2025: XDR Matures</div>
                <p>
                    XDR platforms become genuinely useful. Native XDR from Microsoft, Palo Alto, and others offers
                    tight integration. Open XDR vendors enable multi-vendor correlation. SIEM/XDR convergence
                    begins.
                </p>
            </div>
        </div>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Marketing vs. Reality</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                Many vendors simply rebranded their SIEM or EDR products as "XDR." True XDR should provide unified
                detection logic, automated correlation, and integrated response—not just log aggregation.
                Ask for proof of concept before buying.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="real-attacks">6. How Each Handles Real Attacks</h2>
        <p>
            Let's examine how EDR and XDR would handle a realistic business email compromise (BEC) attack:
        </p>

        <h3>Attack Scenario: Executive Impersonation</h3>
        <ol>
            <li>Attacker sends phishing email impersonating the CFO to accounts payable</li>
            <li>Employee clicks link, enters credentials on fake Microsoft login page</li>
            <li>Attacker logs in from different country using stolen credentials</li>
            <li>Attacker creates mailbox rule to hide sent emails</li>
            <li>Attacker requests wire transfer to "new vendor"</li>
        </ol>

        <h4>EDR Response</h4>
        <p>
            EDR visibility is <strong>limited</strong> in this scenario. The attack happens primarily in the cloud
            (email, M365) with no malware on the endpoint. EDR might detect:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li>Browser navigating to suspicious domain (if URL inspection is enabled)</li>
            <li>Credential input on non-corporate site (limited visibility)</li>
        </ul>
        <p>
            <strong>Verdict:</strong> EDR alone misses 80% of this attack. The credential theft, impossible travel,
            mailbox manipulation, and fraudulent communication all occur outside endpoint visibility.
        </p>

        <h4>XDR Response</h4>
        <p>
            XDR correlates across layers and detects the full attack chain:
        </p>
        <ul>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> <strong>Email
                    layer:</strong> Phishing email flagged based on sender reputation and link analysis</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> <strong>Identity
                    layer:</strong> Impossible travel alert (login from different country)</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i> <strong>Cloud
                    layer:</strong> New mailbox rule creation flagged as suspicious</li>
            <li><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-green);"></i>
                <strong>Correlation:</strong> Links phishing email → credential entry → suspicious login → mailbox
                changes
            </li>
        </ul>
        <p>
            <strong>Verdict:</strong> XDR detects and correlates the attack, enabling response before financial
            loss.
        </p>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> When EDR Wins</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                For ransomware attacks that execute on endpoints, EDR often provides faster detection and
                response than XDR. The attack happens where EDR has deepest visibility, and endpoint isolation
                can stop lateral movement immediately.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="hidden-costs">7. The Hidden Costs Nobody Talks About</h2>
        <p>
            Vendor pricing is just the beginning. Here are the real costs security leaders discover after
            deployment:
        </p>

        <h3>EDR Hidden Costs</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Cost Category</th>
                    <th>Reality</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Alert Fatigue</strong></td>
                    <td>Without correlation, analysts spend hours connecting EDR alerts to network and cloud events
                        manually</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Blind Spots</strong></td>
                    <td>Cloud-native attacks, email threats, and identity attacks require separate tools and
                        processes</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Integration Overhead</strong></td>
                    <td>If you later need XDR-like correlation, building it yourself with SIEM is expensive and
                        complex</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>XDR Hidden Costs</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Cost Category</th>
                    <th>Reality</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Integration Complexity</strong></td>
                    <td>Native XDR requires vendor ecosystem buy-in; Open XDR requires ongoing API maintenance</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Tuning Time</strong></td>
                    <td>Cross-domain correlation creates new false positive categories; expect 3-6 months of tuning
                    </td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Data Ingestion</strong></td>
                    <td>Some XDR platforms charge per GB ingested; cloud logs can be surprisingly expensive</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Staffing Requirements</strong></td>
                    <td>XDR correlation only helps if staff can investigate cross-domain incidents; training is
                        essential</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Vendor Lock-in</strong></td>
                    <td>Native XDR creates deep dependency on single vendor's roadmap and pricing decisions</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="decision-framework">8. Decision Framework: Which One Do You Actually Need?</h2>

        <div class="decision-box">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-cyan);"></i> Choose EDR When:</h3>

            <div class="decision-item choose-edr">
                <i class="fas fa-building"></i>
                <div>
                    <strong>Organization Size: SMB (Under 500 Employees)</strong>
                    <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary);">Limited security team bandwidth means
                        simpler is better. EDR provides excellent protection without integration overhead.</p>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="decision-item choose-edr">
                <i class="fas fa-server"></i>
                <div>
                    <strong>Infrastructure: Primarily On-Premises</strong>
                    <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary);">If most workloads run on endpoints and
                        on-prem servers, XDR's cloud visibility provides less value.</p>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="decision-item choose-edr">
                <i class="fas fa-dollar-sign"></i>
                <div>
                    <strong>Budget: Under $100K Annual Security Tooling</strong>
                    <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary);">EDR provides the best protection per dollar
                        for constrained budgets. Invest in tuning before expanding scope.</p>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="decision-item choose-edr">
                <i class="fas fa-user"></i>
                <div>
                    <strong>Team: 1-3 Security Staff</strong>
                    <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary);">XDR generates cross-domain investigations
                        that require skilled analysts. Start with EDR mastery.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>

        <div class="decision-box">
            <h3><i class="fas fa-check-circle" style="color: var(--accent-blue);"></i> Choose XDR When:</h3>

            <div class="decision-item choose-xdr">
                <i class="fas fa-cloud"></i>
                <div>
                    <strong>Environment: Heavy Cloud/SaaS Usage</strong>
                    <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary);">If M365, AWS, Azure, or SaaS apps hold
                        critical data, XDR's cloud visibility is essential for threat detection.</p>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="decision-item choose-xdr">
                <i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i>
                <div>
                    <strong>Threat Profile: Targeted by Sophisticated Adversaries</strong>
                    <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary);">Nation-state actors and advanced persistent
                        threats (APTs) use multi-stage attacks that XDR is designed to detect.</p>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="decision-item choose-xdr">
                <i class="fas fa-users"></i>
                <div>
                    <strong>Team: Established SOC with 5+ Analysts</strong>
                    <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary);">XDR's cross-domain correlation helps mature
                        teams investigate faster. But immature teams get overwhelmed.</p>
                </div>
            </div>

            <div class="decision-item choose-xdr">
                <i class="fas fa-balance-scale"></i>
                <div>
                    <strong>Compliance: Heavy Regulatory Requirements</strong>
                    <p style="margin: 0; color: var(--text-secondary);">Regulations like DORA and NIS2 require
                        cross-domain logging and correlation. XDR helps meet requirements.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
        </div>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> The Phased Approach</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                Many organizations start with <strong>EDR + MDR</strong> (Managed Detection and Response) to build
                maturity,
                then transition to <strong>XDR</strong> as their team and infrastructure grows. Don't skip
                steps—each phase
                builds operational skills for the next.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="vendor-landscape">9. The Vendor Landscape in 2025</h2>

        <h3>Leading EDR Vendors</h3>
        <div class="vendor-grid">
            <div class="vendor-card">
                <h4>CrowdStrike Falcon</h4>
                <div class="vendor-type">Cloud-Native EDR</div>
                <p>Industry leader in endpoint protection. Lightweight agent, excellent threat intelligence, strong
                    MDR option. Premium pricing.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="vendor-card">
                <h4>SentinelOne</h4>
                <div class="vendor-type">AI-Powered EDR</div>
                <p>Autonomous response capabilities, strong ransomware protection. Competitive alternative to
                    CrowdStrike.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="vendor-card">
                <h4>Microsoft Defender for Endpoint</h4>
                <div class="vendor-type">Enterprise EDR</div>
                <p>Excellent for M365-heavy environments. Lower cost for E5 license holders. Tight Azure AD
                    integration.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="vendor-card">
                <h4>Carbon Black (VMware)</h4>
                <div class="vendor-type">Hybrid EDR</div>
                <p>Strong for hybrid environments with VMware infrastructure. Acquired by Broadcom; future
                    uncertain.</p>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h3>Leading XDR Vendors</h3>
        <div class="vendor-grid">
            <div class="vendor-card">
                <h4>Microsoft Sentinel + Defender XDR</h4>
                <div class="vendor-type">Native XDR (Microsoft Ecosystem)</div>
                <p>Best-in-class for M365/Azure shops. Unified portal, strong identity protection. Requires
                    Microsoft commitment.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="vendor-card">
                <h4>Palo Alto Cortex XDR</h4>
                <div class="vendor-type">Native XDR (Network-Centric)</div>
                <p>Excellent network + endpoint correlation. Strong for Palo Alto firewall customers. Premium
                    pricing.</p>
            </div>
            <div class="vendor-card">
                <h4>Trend Micro Vision One</h4>
                <div class="vendor-type">Hybrid XDR</div>
                <p>Good cross-domain coverage including email. Strong for midmarket orgs with mixed environments.
                </p>
            </div>
            <div class="vendor-card">
                <h4>CrowdStrike Falcon XDR</h4>
                <div class="vendor-type">Expanded EDR</div>
                <p>Adds cloud and identity visibility to Falcon EDR. Maintains CrowdStrike's endpoint strengths.</p>
            </div>
        </div>

        <h2 id="migration-path">10. The Migration Path: EDR to XDR</h2>
        <p>
            If you decide to transition from EDR to XDR, here's a practical roadmap:
        </p>

        <h3>Phase 1: Foundation (Months 1-3)</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Ensure EDR is fully deployed and tuned with minimal false positives</li>
            <li>Document current detection coverage and known blind spots</li>
            <li>Inventory all security data sources (cloud, email, identity)</li>
            <li>Assess vendor options based on existing stack</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Phase 2: Integration (Months 4-6)</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Connect priority data sources (typically cloud identity first)</li>
            <li>Enable cross-domain correlation rules gradually</li>
            <li>Train analysts on multi-domain investigations</li>
            <li>Tune correlation logic to reduce false positives</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Phase 3: Optimization (Months 7-12)</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Add remaining data sources (network, email, applications)</li>
            <li>Build custom detection rules for organization-specific threats</li>
            <li>Implement automated response playbooks</li>
            <li>Measure and report on improved detection and response metrics</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Common Migration Mistake</strong>
            <p style="margin: 0;">
                Don't enable all XDR data sources and correlation rules simultaneously. The alert volume will
                overwhelm your team. Add one data source at a time, tune it, then proceed.
            </p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="key-takeaways">11. Key Takeaways</h2>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Summary: When to Choose Each</strong>
            <ul style="margin: 1rem 0 0 0; padding-left: 1.2rem;">
                <li><strong>Choose EDR</strong> if you're an SMB, have limited security staff, operate primarily
                    on-premises, or need to maximize protection per dollar spent</li>
                <li><strong>Choose XDR</strong> if you have significant cloud/SaaS footprint, face sophisticated
                    threat actors, have a mature SOC, or need cross-domain regulatory logging</li>
                <li><strong>Consider EDR + MDR</strong> as an intermediate step to build operational maturity before
                    XDR</li>
                <li><strong>Evaluate Native vs Open XDR</strong> based on your existing vendor ecosystem and
                    integration requirements</li>
            </ul>
        </div>

        <p>
            The best security solution is one your team can actually operate effectively. A fully utilized EDR
            deployment beats a poorly managed XDR every time. Focus on operational maturity, then expand scope.
        </p>
